summary: Describes a simple username and password authentication method for the SOCKS version 5 setup. It fits into the authentication subnegotiation framework that SOCKS5 defines.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a SOCKS version 5 login exchange using a username and password. The request carries the password in cleartext, so the RFC advises against it where traffic can be sniffed.

questions: how does socks5 username password authentication work
what is socks5 username password authentication
is socks5 password sent in cleartext
subtitle: A username-and-password method for the SOCKS version 5 authentication exchange.

tldr.problem: SOCKS version 5 allows authentication methods during connection setup and needs concrete methods that fit its subnegotiation.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a version, username length and value, and password length and value; the server returns a status byte.
tldr.outcome: A nonzero failure status requires the server to close the connection, and the password is sent in cleartext.

today: RFC 1929 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Where the Method Fits
sections.content:
SOCKS version 5 provides a framework for arbitrary authentication methods during the initial connection setup. This RFC specifies one such method: a username-and-password subnegotiation that begins after the client selects it.

The packet diagrams give field lengths in octets. A field marked with a specific hexadecimal value must contain that value.
sections.plainLanguage: SOCKS version 5 can use different ways to check a user's identity. This document defines one way based on a username and password.

sections.title: Request and Server Response
sections.content:
The client request contains VER, ULEN, UNAME, PLEN, and PASSWD. The version is X'01'; the username and password each have a one-octet length field and a value from 1 to 255 octets.

The server verifies the values and replies with a version and a one-octet status. X'00' means success. Any other status means failure, and the server MUST close the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The client sends the username and password with their lengths. The server answers with a success or failure code and closes the connection after a failure.

sections.title: Cleartext Password Warning
sections.content:
The username/password request carries the password in cleartext. The RFC says this subnegotiation is not recommended in environments where sniffing is possible and practical.

The document describes the authentication exchange but does not define a way to encrypt the password within the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The password is readable in the data sent over the connection. Someone able to monitor that traffic could see it.
